subject: Chemistry
title: The Chemistry of Tears
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Chemistry of Tears.

hook.text: You produce three different types of tears, and each has a different chemical composition.

buildup.text: Basal tears lubricate your eyes. They contain water, oils, mucus, and lysozyme—an antibacterial enzyme.

discovery.text: Reflex tears flush irritants. They contain more water and antibodies than basal tears.

twist.text: Emotional tears contain stress hormones like leucine enkephalin. Crying may literally flush out stress chemicals.

climax.text: Under a microscope, dried tears from different emotions form unique crystal patterns. Each cry looks different.

punchline.text: Three types of tears, three recipes. Even crying is chemistry.

quiz.question: What makes emotional tears chemically different from other tears?
options: They contain stress hormones not found in basal or reflex tears
They contain more salt than other tears
They are produced by different glands

details.summary: Tears are a complex chemical solution containing water, salts, lipids, mucins, lysozyme antibacterial enzyme, and immunoglobulins. The body produces three types: basal tears for lubrication, reflex tears for irritant removal.
details.whyItMatters: Tear chemistry reveals that emotional crying is chemically distinct from reflex crying, suggesting that emotional tears may serve a unique biochemical stress-relief function.
takeaways: Emotional tears contain higher levels of stress hormones than reflex tears
Lysozyme in tears kills bacteria and protects the eye from infection
The three-layer tear film includes lipid, aqueous, and mucin layers

faq.question: Why do emotional tears have a different chemical composition?
faq.answer: Emotional tears contain elevated levels of leucine enkephalin (a natural painkiller), adrenocorticotropic hormone (a stress marker), and prolactin..

faq.question: How does lysozyme in tears protect against infection?
faq.answer: Lysozyme is an enzyme that breaks down the cell walls of bacteria by cleaving the bond between N-acetylmuramic acid and N-acetylglucosamine in peptidoglycan. This destroys the structural integrity of bacterial cells, killing them before they can infect the vulnerable surface of the eye.
